assertions.description: The two-value overflow shorthand is the syntax this feature extends; without it there is no pair to talk about.
The reference behaviour: overflow:clip on both axes produces an element that clips without scrolling, proved by assigning a scroll offset and reading back zero.
The fact that makes this feature necessary: overflow:hidden is scrollable, it just has no scrollbar. An axis coerced from clip to hidden therefore still carries a scroll offset.

The long-standing coercion that clip's used to mirror: visible next to a scrollable value computes to auto. It is asserted here so the demos can present the clip rule as a change to one half of a symmetric pair rather than a new invention.
The feature itself: with overflow:scroll clip, the block axis computes to clip rather than being coerced to hidden.

Computed style is not the point on its own — the consequence is. With overflow:scroll clip the inline axis must still take a scroll offset and the block axis must refuse one, which is what stops a focused element from displacing content on an axis with no scrollbar.

overflow-x:scroll with overflow-y:clip must compute exactly as the shorthand does. A coercion that applied to one spelling and not the other would be a trap, and the demos measure both spellings because of it.
assertions.test: (()=>{try{const b=document.createElement('div');b.style.cssText='position:absolute;left:-10000px;width:100px;height:100px;overflow-x:scroll;overflow-y:clip';document.body.append(b);const s=getComputedStyle(b);const pair=s.overflowX+' '+s.overflowY;b.remove();const c=document.createElement('div');c.style.cssText='position:absolute;left:-10000px;width:100px;height:100px;overflow:scroll clip';document.body.append(c);const cs=getComputedStyle(c);const shorthand=cs.overflowX+' '+cs.overflowY;c.remove();return pair===shorthand;}catch(e){return false;}})()
